title: Expression Add Operators
description: Brute force to optimized: evaluating full expression strings from scratch versus backtracking with incremental value and previous-operand tracking for correct operator precedence.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string num containing only digits, and an integer target, return all possible ways to insert the binary operators "+", "-", and "*" between the digits of num so that the resulting expression evaluates to target. Numbers in the expression cannot have leading zeros (except the number "0" itself), and standard operator precedence (multiplication before addition/subtraction) applies.

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Insert operators between characters to reach a target value\"","Backtracking: choose a split point for the next number, choose an operator, recurse"],["Multiplication has different precedence than addition/subtraction","Track the PREVIOUS operand separately so a multiplication can retroactively adjust the running total"]]}

blocks.text: Digits must be used in their original left-to-right order, grouped into one or more consecutive digits to form each number in the expression, with an operator placed between consecutive numbers. The challenge is correctly handling multiplication's higher precedence when building the running total incrementally.

blocks.title: Analogy: Filling in Missing Math Symbols
blocks.text: Picture a sequence of digits with the plus, minus, and multiply signs erased, and being asked to restore every possible way of filling them back in so the equation balances to a target number, remembering that multiplication binds tighter than addition or subtraction.

blocks.caption: At each step, choose how many digits form the next number, then choose the operator before it

blocks.text: Before evaluating full expression strings after building them, notice that maintaining a running value ALONGSIDE the value of the most recently added operand lets multiplication be handled incrementally: instead of re-evaluating everything, undo the previous operand's contribution and reapply it multiplied by the new number.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Building the expression digit group by digit group requires choosing, at each step, how many digits form the next number (its length), and (for all but the first number) which operator precedes it.

Observation 2: A number with a leading zero is only valid if it IS zero itself (a single "0"); "05" or "00" as multi-digit numbers are invalid, so any split producing a multi-digit number starting with "0" must be skipped.

Observation 3: For plus and minus, the running value simply increases or decreases by the new number's value, and the "previous operand" for future multiplication purposes becomes plus or minus that new number.

Observation 4: For multiplication, the running value must first have the previous operand's contribution REMOVED (since it was already added or subtracted), then the product of the previous operand and the new number ADDED back in, and the new "previous operand" becomes that product (so a THIRD consecutive multiplication continues to compound correctly).

This leads to backtracking over every possible next-number length and every operator choice, maintaining both a running total and the value of the last operand actually applied, so multiplication can retroactively correct the running total in O(1) per step.

Enumerate every way to insert operators between EVERY pair of adjacent digits (fixing the digit grouping to single digits only would miss valid multi-digit numbers, so instead enumerate every possible digit grouping AND every operator choice, then evaluate the full expression string using standard precedence rules at the end).

items: Generate every way to partition num into consecutive digit groups (every possible set of split points).
For each partition, try every combination of "+", "-", "*" between the resulting numbers.
Fully evaluate each candidate expression string (respecting precedence) and keep those equal to target.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Building the full expression string first, then parsing and evaluating it from scratch, repeats work that could instead be tracked incrementally during construction.
This still correctly respects operator precedence, but at the cost of redundant re-evaluation for every candidate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(4^n times n), roughly 3 operator choices times digit-grouping choices, each requiring an O(n) evaluation pass.
Space: O(n) for the expression string and recursion.

Limitation: evaluating the full expression from scratch for every candidate is unnecessary; tracking the running value AND the previous operand incrementally during construction lets multiplication be applied correctly in O(1) per step, without a separate evaluation pass.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-evaluating from scratch is wasteful: the running total after placing the first k numbers does not need to be recomputed once a (k+1)-th number and operator are chosen; only the CHANGE needs to be applied.

The key trick for multiplication: since value = ... + prev (or ... - prev) already includes the previous operand's contribution added at face value, applying a multiplication instead requires first subtracting prev back out, then adding prev*cur in its place, which correctly "retroactively" upgrades the previous term's contribution to reflect the multiplication.

Handling addition and subtraction: these simply adjust the running value directly by the new number (added or subtracted), with the new "previous operand" becoming plus or minus that new number, for the potential next multiplication to reference.

The core idea: track (running value, previous operand value) as recursive state, updating both correctly for each of the three operator choices, avoiding any separate expression-parsing step.

Backtrack over the next number's digit length (skipping invalid leading-zero groupings) and operator choice, incrementally updating the running value and previous operand exactly as derived above, recording the built expression string once all digits are used and the running value equals target.
Dry run for num = "123", target = 6, path "1*2*3"

blocks.caption: Track running value and previous operand; multiplication undoes the previous contribution and reapplies it multiplied

blocks.text: Tracking the previous operand separately from the running value allows multiplication to be applied correctly without re-parsing the whole expression: since the previous operand's value was already folded into the running total (added or subtracted), subtracting it back out and adding the product in its place exactly reproduces what standard precedence rules would compute, but incrementally and in O(1) per step.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(4^n), each position can branch into digit-length choices times 3 operators, bounded by n digits.
Space: O(n) recursion depth and path string.

blocks.text: Expression Add Operators is a strong example of tracking auxiliary state (the previous operand) during backtracking specifically to handle an operator with different precedence (multiplication) without needing to re-parse or re-evaluate the whole expression from scratch.

items: Forgetting the no-leading-zero rule for multi-digit numbers (e.g., "05" is invalid, but "0" alone is valid).
Applying multiplication as if it had the same precedence as addition/subtraction, without the undo-and-reapply trick for the previous operand.

blocks.text: Clearly explaining the "undo the previous operand, then reapply it multiplied" trick before coding demonstrates a solid grasp of how to handle operator precedence incrementally, which is the crux of this problem's difficulty.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "insert operators to reach a target, respecting precedence", think: backtrack while tracking the running value AND the previous operand, so multiplication can retroactively adjust the total.

items: How would you support parentheses as an additional operator choice?
How would you count the number of valid expressions without generating all of them explicitly?
Basic Calculator style problems, which use the same "track previous operand for multiplication precedence" trick during expression evaluation.
Any backtracking problem needing incremental state beyond just the running total, to correctly undo and reapply a prior contribution.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches share the same exponential branching factor from digit groupings and operator choices; the incremental value/prev tracking approach avoids the extra O(n) re-evaluation cost per candidate that full re-parsing would require.

items: Pattern: backtracking with auxiliary state (previous operand) to handle an operator of different precedence incrementally.
Core Idea: at each step, choose the next number's digit length and an operator; for multiplication, undo the previous operand's contribution and reapply it multiplied by the new number.
Time: O(4^n times n) for the full-evaluation brute force, O(4^n) for the optimized incremental approach.
Space: O(n) recursion depth and path for both.
Most Important Observation: tracking the previous operand alongside the running value lets multiplication be applied in O(1) without re-parsing the expression.
Interview Difficulty: a genuinely tricky backtracking problem due to the operator precedence handling.
One line memory trick: track value and previous operand; multiplication undoes and reapplies the previous term.
